  • B after trading: 5mn phones and 35mn bags. Alone, making 5mn phones would leave it 60 − (5 × 6) = 30mn bags. Gain: 5mn bags.

Both consume beyond their own PPF. Both gain as long as a phone swaps for between 3 and 6 bags.

cards.front:
Define exports, imports, visible trade and invisible trade. Classify each for the UK:

(a) an American tourist spending money in London; (b) a UK family on holiday in Spain; (c) a UK carmaker selling cars in France; (d) a UK supermarket buying bananas from Colombia.
cards.back:
Exports — goods and services produced in one country and sold to buyers in another, so money flows into the exporting country.

Imports — goods and services bought from another country, so money flows out.

Visible trade — trade in goods, things you can see and touch, such as cars, medicines or oil.

Invisible trade — trade in services, such as banking, insurance, tourism and education.

  • (a) Invisible export: money comes into the UK.
  • (b) Invisible import: money goes out.
  • (c) Visible export.
  • (d) Visible import.

What matters is which way the money flows, not where the people go. The UK imports more goods than it exports but exports more services than it imports.

source.verbatim: trade in goods, things you can see and touch, such as cars, medicines or oil.

cards.front: Define a trading bloc. Then build the chains of reasoning: how can international trade raise a country's economic growth, and what limits the gain?
cards.back:
Trading bloc — a group of countries that agree to reduce or remove barriers to trade between themselves, such as the EU. Firms inside a bloc can sell to the other members without tariffs, which gives them a larger home market.

  • Exports: foreign demand for UK goods rises → UK firms sell more and expand output → they hire more workers, whose spending raises demand further → higher real GDP.
  • Bigger markets: firms sell to the world, not just one country → they produce on a larger scale → economies of scale lower their average costs → more competitive prices and higher profits to invest.
  • Competition: imports compete with home producers → firms must cut costs and improve products to survive → higher productivity, which raises the economy's capacity to grow.

The gain depends on:

  • Imports as well as exports: spending on imports leaves the country, so if imports replace home production, the gain from exports is partly offset.
  • What the country exports: a country relying on raw materials, whose prices swing widely, gets less steady growth than one exporting a mix of goods and services.

source.verbatim: a group of countries that agree to reduce or remove barriers to trade between themselves, such as the EU.

cards.front: Cheap imported clothes and electronics flood into the UK. Evaluate the effect on UK standards of living.
cards.back:
Standard of living — the quantity and quality of goods and services people can afford, which depends on their real income.

  • Consumers gain: imports cost less → each pound buys more → real incomes rise → a higher standard of living, with more choice too.
  • Firms using imported inputs gain: cheaper materials and components → lower costs → lower prices for their own customers, or higher profit.
  • Competing UK producers lose: cheap imports win customers from them → sales and profits fall → factories close and jobs go → lower incomes for workers in those industries and the towns that depend on them.

It depends on:

  • Whether workers find new jobs: if they can retrain or move into growing industries, the loss is short term. If their skills don't fit and the jobs are elsewhere, they can stay unemployed for years.
  • Why the imports are cheap: low prices from lower costs or better methods are a genuine gain. Prices kept low by poor safety standards, or by selling below cost to win a market, can hurt consumers and UK firms later.

Judgement: consumers gain, but the losses fall on particular workers and towns. Living standards rise overall when the imports are cheap because they are made at lower cost, and when the workers who lose their jobs can move into growing industries.

source.verbatim: the quantity and quality of goods and services people can afford, which depends on their real income.

cards.front: Define appreciation and depreciation. What decides the value of the pound?
cards.back:
Appreciation — a rise in the value of a currency against another, such as the pound rising from $1.30 to $1.40.

Depreciation — a fall in the value of a currency against another, such as the pound falling from $1.30 to $1.20.

The pound has a floating exchange rate: its value is set by the demand for and supply of pounds on the foreign exchange market.

  • Pounds are demanded by anyone abroad who needs them: foreign buyers of UK goods and services, foreign firms investing in the UK, and savers moving money into UK banks.
  • Pounds are supplied by UK households and firms changing them into other currencies to buy imports or invest abroad.

Check which way round the rate is written. If £1 = $1.30, a higher number means a stronger pound. If $1 = £0.77, a higher number means a weaker pound.

source.verbatim: a rise in the value of a currency against another, such as the pound rising from $1.30 to $1.40.

cards.front: Sketch the market for pounds showing an appreciation. Give three things that could cause it.
cards.back:
The exchange rate goes up the side and the quantity of pounds along the bottom. Demand for pounds shifts right from D1 to D2 along an unchanged supply curve S. The exchange rate rises from P1 to P2, and the quantity of pounds rises from Q1 to Q2.

  • Interest rates: UK rates rise compared with rates abroad → saving in the UK pays more → foreign savers buy pounds → demand for pounds rises.
  • Demand for exports: foreign demand for UK goods rises → buyers need more pounds to pay for them → demand for pounds rises.
  • Speculation: traders expect the pound to rise → they buy it now to profit later → demand for pounds rises.
cards.svgAlt: Market for pounds with exchange rate on the vertical axis and quantity of pounds on the horizontal axis; demand shifts right from D1 to D2 along an unchanged supply curve S, so the exchange rate rises from P1 to P2 and quantity rises from Q1 to Q2

cards.front: Sketch the market for pounds showing a depreciation caused by an increase in the supply of pounds. What could cause the increase?
cards.back:
The exchange rate goes up the side and the quantity of pounds along the bottom. Supply of pounds shifts right from S1 to S2 along an unchanged demand curve D. The exchange rate falls from P1 to P2, while the quantity of pounds rises from Q1 to Q2.

  • Spending on imports: UK spending on imports rises → UK households and firms change more pounds into other currencies to pay for them → supply of pounds rises.
  • Speculation: traders expect the pound to fall → they sell it → supply of pounds rises.
cards.svgAlt: Market for pounds with exchange rate on the vertical axis and quantity of pounds on the horizontal axis; supply shifts right from S1 to S2 along an unchanged demand curve D, so the exchange rate falls from P1 to P2 and quantity rises from Q1 to Q2

cards.front:
The exchange rate moves from £1 = €1.20 to £1 = €1.05.

(a) Calculate the percentage change, and say whether the pound has appreciated or depreciated. (b) Convert a UK firm's £40 kettle into euros at each rate. (c) Convert the sterling cost of a €600 component the firm imports at each rate.
cards.back:
• (a) (1.05 − 1.20) ÷ 1.20 × 100 = −12.5%. Each pound buys fewer euros, so the pound has depreciated.
  • (b) Multiply by the rate: 40 × 1.20 = €48, then 40 × 1.05 = €42. The kettle is 12.5% cheaper for buyers paying in euros.
  • (c) Divide by the rate: 600 ÷ 1.20 = £500, then 600 ÷ 1.05 = £571. The component is about 14.3% dearer for the UK firm.

The firm's exports become more price competitive, but its imported components cost more. The net effect depends on which is larger.

cards.front: Define the effective exchange rate. The sterling effective exchange rate index falls from 90 to 81. What does this tell you, and why might a single firm need more than this?
cards.back:
Effective exchange rate — the value of a currency against a basket of other currencies, with each weighted by how much the country trades with it. It is also called the trade-weighted exchange rate.

  • Why it is needed: the pound can rise against the dollar while falling against the euro, so no single exchange rate shows whether it is stronger overall.
  • The fall: (81 − 90) ÷ 90 × 100 = −10%. The pound has depreciated by 10% on average against the currencies of the UK's trading partners.
  • The level: the Bank of England's index has January 2005 = 100, so 81 means the pound is worth 19% less on average than then.

The effective rate shows what is happening to UK firms as a whole. A single firm still needs the rate for the currency it actually trades in: an exporter selling only to the US cares about the dollar.

source.verbatim: the value of a currency against a basket of other currencies, with each weighted by how much the country trades with it. It is also called the trade-weighted exchange rate.

cards.front: The pound depreciates sharply. Evaluate the impact on UK firms.
cards.back:
• Exporters gain: each UK product costs less in foreign currency → the firm can cut its foreign price and win more sales, or keep the price and earn more pounds on each one → higher revenue and profit.
  • Importers lose: materials and components priced in dollars or euros cost more pounds → higher unit costs → the firm raises its prices and loses some sales, or keeps its prices and accepts a lower margin.
  • Firms competing with imports gain: imported rivals cost more in UK shops → customers switch to UK-made products → higher sales for UK producers.

It depends on:

  • How much the firm imports as well as exports: many exporters buy parts from abroad, so a weaker pound raises their costs while it helps their sales. The net effect depends on which is larger.
  • Price elasticity of demand: if foreign buyers are price-sensitive, a lower foreign price wins many extra sales. A strong brand sells on quality, so the exchange rate matters less.
  • Size and duration of the change: firms rarely switch suppliers or markets over a brief dip. A big fall that persists for a year or more can make them rethink where they source parts and which countries they target.

Judgement: the biggest winners export price-sensitive products, or compete with imports, and buy their inputs in the UK. The biggest losers buy most of their inputs abroad and export little.

cards.front: Define the economic cycle and the trend rate of growth. What drives the cycle?
cards.back:
Economic cycle — the repeated rise and fall in economic activity, measured by real GDP, around the economy's long-term trend. It is also called the trade cycle or business cycle.

Trend rate of growth — the average rate at which real GDP grows over many years, as the economy's capacity to produce rises.

Real GDP is the value of everything an economy produces, adjusted for inflation. Actual growth rarely matches the trend: some years it runs faster, some slower, and sometimes output falls.

What drives it: mainly changes in spending, and each change feeds on itself. Confidence rises → households and firms spend and invest more → firms raise output and hire → incomes rise → spending rises again. A fall in confidence, a rise in interest rates or a sudden shock, such as a jump in energy prices, runs the same chain downwards.

source.verbatim: the repeated rise and fall in economic activity, measured by real GDP, around the economy's long-term trend. It is also called the trade cycle or business cycle.

cards.front: Define a boom and a recession, and compare what you would expect to see in each. If growth falls from 4% to 2%, is that a recession?
cards.back:
Boom — a period when real GDP grows faster than its trend rate and the economy is working at or near full capacity.

Recession — a fall in real GDP for two consecutive quarters, that is, six months of negative economic growth.

  • Output: in a boom, real GDP rises above its trend rate. In a recession it shrinks, and firms have spare capacity.
  • Unemployment: low in a boom, when firms struggle to fill vacancies and skills shortages appear. Rising in a recession, as firms cut jobs.
  • Inflation: rising in a boom, as spending outgrows what firms can supply. Low in a recession, and prices can even fall.
  • Confidence: high in a boom, so households borrow and firms invest. Low in a recession, so households save more and firms put off investment.
  • Imports: more in a boom and fewer in a recession, as incomes rise and fall.
  • Government finances: stronger in a boom. Weaker in a recession, as tax revenue falls and benefit spending rises, so borrowing goes up.

4% to 2% is not a recession. The economy is still growing, so real GDP is higher than a year ago. A recession needs real GDP itself to fall.

source.verbatim: a period when real GDP grows faster than its trend rate and the economy is working at or near full capacity.

cards.front: Sketch the economic cycle around the trend rate of growth. Label and describe its four phases.
cards.back:
Real GDP goes up the side and time along the bottom. The trend rate of growth is a straight upward line, and actual output curves above and below it.

  • Boom (or peak): output grows faster than the trend and the economy works close to its full capacity. Output is above the trend line.
  • Downturn (or slowdown): growth slows, and output drops back towards the trend.
  • Recession (or slump): output falls, leaving the economy well below what it could produce. Its lowest point is called the trough.
  • Recovery (or upturn, expansion): growth returns and output climbs back towards the trend.
cards.svgAlt: Real GDP on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis; a straight upward line is labelled trend rate of growth, and actual output curves above it in a shaded area labelled boom, crosses back through it at the point labelled downturn, dips below it in a shaded area labelled recession, and rises back to it at the point labelled recovery

cards.front: Build the chains of reasoning: how do a boom and a recession affect a firm's costs, capacity and cash?
cards.back:
In a boom:

  • Costs rise: firms compete for scarce staff and materials → wages and input prices go up → higher unit costs → margins shrink unless prices rise too.
  • Capacity runs short: orders outgrow output → delivery times lengthen → customers go to rivals → lost sales unless the firm invests or hires.

In a recession:

  • Cash gets tight: customers pay later and banks lend more cautiously → less cash coming in → firms struggle to pay suppliers and staff → a risk of failure, even for firms that were profitable.
  • Some costs fall: more people are looking for work → easier to recruit and less pressure on pay → lower labour costs. Rents and material prices may ease too.

Most firms sell more in a boom and less in a recession, but their costs tend to rise in a boom and ease in a recession.

cards.front: Evaluate how a firm might respond as the economy moves from boom into recession. What decides how hard it is hit?
cards.back:
How firms respond to a recession:

  • Prices: hold or cut prices, and run promotions.
  • Output and stock: cut output and run stock down.
  • Staff: freeze hiring, cut hours or make redundancies.
  • Investment: delay projects and close loss-making sites.
  • Products: push value ranges and smaller pack sizes.

What decides how hard it is hit:

  • What it sells: sellers of luxuries feel each swing most and sellers of necessities least. Sellers of inferior goods move the opposite way.
  • How much it borrows: a firm with large debts struggles when sales fall and when rates rise. One with cash reserves can ride out a recession, and even buy weaker rivals cheaply.
  • How deep and long the recession is: a short, mild slowdown can be absorbed with stock and cash. A long recession forces job cuts and closures.

Judgement: a firm with little debt that sells necessities or value ranges is hit least, and may even gain. The deeper and longer the recession, the more even a strong firm has to cut jobs and capacity.

cards.front: Sketch the circular flow of income between households and firms. Why should output, income and expenditure give the same answer?
cards.back:
Circular flow of income — a model of how money moves round an economy, from firms to households as income and back to firms as spending.

Firms are at the top and households at the bottom.

  • Households to firms: households own the factors of production (land, labour, capital and enterprise), and firms hire them. Households also spend their income on firms' goods and services.
  • Firms to households: firms pay for the factors with income (rent, wages, interest and profit), and supply goods and services.

Each money flow pays for a real flow going the other way: income pays for the factors of production, and spending pays for the goods and services.

Output, income and expenditure are three ways of measuring national income, the size of the economy. In theory they match, because every pound spent on a product is a pound of income for whoever helped make it.
cards.svgAlt: Circular flow with firms at the top and households at the bottom; on the right an arrow runs from firms to households, labelled goods and services inside the circle and income (rent, wages, interest, profit) outside it; on the left an arrow runs from households to firms, labelled expenditure on goods and services inside the circle and factors of production (land, labour, capital, enterprise) outside it

source.verbatim: a model of how money moves round an economy, from firms to households as income and back to firms as spending.

cards.front: Define an injection and a withdrawal. Pair each injection with the withdrawal from the same sector, and state when the circular flow is in equilibrium.
cards.back:
Injection — spending that enters the circular flow from outside the household-firm loop: investment, government spending and exports.

Withdrawal — income that leaves the circular flow instead of being spent on the country's own output: saving, taxation and imports. Withdrawals are also called leakages.

  • Financial: investment (I), firms spending on machinery, buildings and equipment, against saving (S), income households put aside instead of spending.
  • Government: government spending (G), on public services such as schools, hospitals and roads, against taxation (T).
  • Overseas: exports (X), spending by foreign buyers on UK goods and services, against imports (M), spending by UK buyers on goods and services from abroad.

Equilibrium: the flow is stable when injections equal withdrawals: I + G + X = S + T + M.

source.verbatim: spending that enters the circular flow from outside the household-firm loop: investment, government spending and exports.

cards.front: Sketch the circular flow with injections and withdrawals. Explain what happens to national income when injections rise above withdrawals, and when withdrawals rise above injections.
cards.back:
Firms are at the top and households at the bottom. Government spending, investment and exports arrow into the circle; taxation, savings and imports arrow out of it.

  • Injections above withdrawals, so the flow grows: foreign demand for UK goods rises → exporters sell more → they take on staff and pay more in wages → those workers spend more in UK shops → sales, output and jobs rise across the economy.
  • Withdrawals above injections, so the flow shrinks: worried households save more → less is spent in shops → firms sell less and cut output and jobs → incomes fall, so spending falls again.

Each round of spending becomes someone else's income, so the final change in national income is bigger than the first one. This is the multiplier effect.

The size of the impact depends on spare capacity (near full capacity, extra spending mostly raises prices) and on where withdrawals go next: banks lend savings on to firms to invest, and taxes pay for government spending, so a withdrawal can come back in as an injection.
cards.svgAlt: Circular flow with firms at the top and households at the bottom; three arrows on the left point into the circle, labelled government spending, investment and exports, and three arrows on the right point out of it, labelled taxation, savings and imports

cards.front: Define aggregate demand and state its formula. What changes each component? Is a rise in the state pension part of G?
cards.back:
Aggregate demand (AD) — total planned spending on a country's goods and services over a period of time. It has four components:

  • Consumption (C): household spending, the largest component. Changed by real incomes, interest rates, confidence about jobs, house prices and how easy it is to borrow.
  • Investment (I): firms' spending on capital goods. Changed by expected future sales, interest rates, retained profit, business confidence and new technology.
  • Government spending (G): on public services and infrastructure. Changed by government priorities, the state of its finances and the economic cycle.
  • Net exports (X − M): exports minus imports. Changed by the exchange rate, incomes at home and abroad, trade barriers, and UK prices and quality compared with rivals'.

A cut in Bank Rate makes borrowing cheaper → households spend more and firms invest more → C and I rise → AD rises.

A pension rise is not G. G is spending on goods and services, such as nurses' pay or a new road. Benefits and state pensions are transfers: the government buys nothing in return. They enter AD only when the people who receive them spend the money, as C.

source.verbatim: total planned spending on a country's goods and services over a period of time. It has four components:

cards.front: Define aggregate supply. Build the chains: how do the cost of inputs and productivity change it?
cards.back:
Aggregate supply (AS) — the total output that firms in an economy are willing and able to produce at each price level.

  • The cost of inputs and resources: wages, energy or raw material prices rise → it costs more to produce each unit → firms raise prices or supply less → AS falls, so output falls and prices rise. Cheaper inputs run the chain the other way, and a weaker pound works like a price rise for firms that import materials.
  • Productivity: better training, equipment or methods → more output from each worker → lower unit costs → firms can supply more at the same prices → AS rises, so output grows without pushing up prices.

The effect depends on how long the change lasts (a short spike in oil prices against a lasting gain in productivity) and how much the input matters: a rise in energy prices hits a steelworks far harder than a software firm.

source.verbatim: the total output that firms in an economy are willing and able to produce at each price level.

cards.front: Define inflation, deflation and disinflation. Inflation falls from 5% to 2%, then from 2% to −0.5%: name each change.
cards.back:
Inflation — a sustained rise in the general level of prices in an economy over time.

Deflation — a sustained fall in the general price level, so the rate of inflation is negative.

Disinflation — a fall in the rate of inflation. Prices are still rising, but more slowly.

The rate of inflation is the percentage rise in the price level over a year.

  • 5% to 2%: disinflation. Prices are still rising, just more slowly.
  • 2% to −0.5%: deflation. Prices are now falling.

source.verbatim: a sustained rise in the general level of prices in an economy over time.

cards.front: What is a price index? How is the CPI built, how does the RPI differ, and how do you turn index numbers into a rate of inflation?
cards.back:
Price index — a number that shows the price level in one period compared with a base period, which is set at 100.

  • CPI: the UK's main measure. The government sets the Bank of England a target of 2% CPI inflation. Each month the ONS records the prices of a basket of goods and services that households typically buy, and weights each item by its share of household spending, so a rise in energy prices moves the index more than a rise in the price of tea.
  • RPI: an older measure. It includes housing costs that the CPI leaves out, such as mortgage interest payments and council tax, and it is usually higher than the CPI. It is still published because some long-term contracts are linked to it.

An index number is not a rate of inflation. To find the rate, take the percentage change in the index from one year to the next.

source.verbatim: a number that shows the price level in one period compared with a base period, which is set at 100.

cards.front:
A gym's revenue is £150,000 in 2023, £162,240 in 2024 and £172,480 in 2025. The price index (2023 = 100) is 104 in 2024 and 112 in 2025.

(a) Calculate the rate of inflation in 2024 and 2025. (b) Calculate real revenue in 2024 and 2025 at 2023 prices. (c) Did the gym really sell more in 2025?
cards.back:
Nominal value — a value measured in the prices of the time, with no adjustment for inflation. Figures at current prices are nominal.

Real value — a value adjusted for inflation, so it shows what has happened to the amount bought or produced. Figures at constant prices are real: they are valued at the prices of one base year.

  • (a) Inflation: 2024: (104 − 100) ÷ 100 × 100 = 4.0%. 2025: (112 − 104) ÷ 104 × 100 = 7.7%, not 8%: divide by the old index, not by 100.
  • (b) Real revenue: 2024: £162,240 ÷ 104 × 100 = £156,000. 2025: £172,480 ÷ 112 × 100 = £154,000.
  • (c) No. At current prices revenue rose 6.3% in 2025, but at constant 2023 prices it fell 1.3%, because prices rose faster than the gym's takings.

source.verbatim: a value measured in the prices of the time, with no adjustment for inflation. Figures at current prices are nominal.

cards.front: Define demand-pull inflation and show it on an AD/AS diagram. What could set it off?
cards.back:
Demand-pull inflation — inflation caused by aggregate demand rising faster than the economy can increase its output.

The price level goes up the side and real GDP along the bottom. AD shifts right from AD1 to AD2 along an upward-sloping SRAS curve. The price level rises from PL1 to PL2, and real GDP rises from Y1 to Y2.

The chain: interest rates are cut, taxes fall or confidence rises → households and firms spend more → firms near full capacity cannot raise output fast enough → they raise prices, and the price level rises.
cards.svgAlt: Price level on the vertical axis and real GDP on the horizontal axis; aggregate demand shifts right from AD1 to AD2 along an upward-sloping SRAS curve, so the price level rises from PL1 to PL2 and real GDP rises from Y1 to Y2

source.verbatim: inflation caused by aggregate demand rising faster than the economy can increase its output.

cards.front: Define cost-push inflation and show it on an AD/AS diagram. How does its effect on output differ from demand-pull inflation?
cards.back:
Cost-push inflation — inflation caused by rising costs of production, which firms pass on as higher prices.

The price level goes up the side and real GDP along the bottom. SRAS shifts left from SRAS1 to SRAS2 along a downward-sloping AD curve. The price level rises from PL1 to PL2, and real GDP falls from Y1 to Y2.

The chain: wages, energy, raw materials or indirect taxes rise, or a weaker pound makes imported inputs dearer → unit costs rise → firms raise prices to protect their margins → the price level rises while output falls.

The difference: demand-pull raises output as well as prices; cost-push cuts output. The two can feed each other: workers ask for higher pay to keep up with prices, which raises firms' costs and pushes prices up again.
cards.svgAlt: Price level on the vertical axis and real GDP on the horizontal axis; short-run aggregate supply shifts left from SRAS1 to SRAS2 along a downward-sloping AD curve, so the price level rises from PL1 to PL2 and real GDP falls from Y1 to Y2

source.verbatim: inflation caused by rising costs of production, which firms pass on as higher prices.

cards.front: Evaluate the impact of high inflation on firms and on individuals. Who loses, who gains, and what decides how much?
cards.back:
Firms:

  • Uncertainty: costs and prices change quickly and unpredictably → firms cannot forecast costs, revenue or the return on a new project with confidence → they put off investment → slower growth and fewer new jobs.
  • Lost competitiveness: UK prices rise faster than rivals' abroad → UK exports look dear and imports look cheap → UK firms lose orders overseas and sales at home.

Individuals:

  • Real income falls when prices rise faster than pay. People on fixed incomes, and those whose pay rises late, are hit hardest. A 2% pay rise with 5% inflation is a real pay cut of about 3%.
  • Savers lose when inflation is above the interest rate on their savings: the money saved buys less each year.
  • Borrowers gain: debts are fixed in pounds, so as prices and wages rise the debt becomes smaller in real terms.

It depends on: how high and predictable inflation is; whether UK inflation is above that in rival countries (a fall in the pound can offset it); whether pay, pensions and benefits keep up; and interest rates. The Bank of England usually raises rates to bring inflation down, which helps savers but makes variable-rate borrowers pay more.

Judgement: steady inflation of about 2% is easy to plan around. High, unpredictable inflation does the most harm, to investment and to anyone whose income does not keep up, and borrowers' gain can be wiped out once interest rates rise.

cards.front:
Define employment, unemployment and underemployment. Is a retired person who is not looking for work unemployed?

31mn people are in work and 1.4mn are unemployed. Calculate the unemployment rate.
cards.back:
Employment — people doing paid work, whether full-time, part-time or self-employed. In UK figures, one hour of paid work a week is enough to count.

Unemployment — people of working age who have no job but are available for work and actively looking for it.

Underemployment — people in work who want more hours than they can get, or whose job makes little use of their skills. A trained chef working ten hours a week in a shop, because that is all she can find, is underemployed.

No. People without a job who are not looking for one, such as full-time students, retired people and carers, are economically inactive, not unemployed.

Unemployment rate: the unemployed as a percentage of everyone in work or looking for it. 1.4 ÷ (31 + 1.4) × 100 = 4.3%. Dividing by the 31mn in work alone gives the wrong answer.

source.verbatim: people of working age who have no job but are available for work and actively looking for it.

cards.front: Compare the claimant count and the ILO measure of unemployment: who counts, where the data comes from, and a strength and weakness of each.
cards.back:
• Claimant count: people claiming benefits because they are out of work: Jobseeker's Allowance, or Universal Credit with a requirement to look for work. It comes from government benefit records.
    • Strength: cheap to collect, monthly, and covers every claimant.
    • Weakness: misses unemployed people who cannot or do not claim, and changes to benefit rules change the count. It also includes some low-paid part-time workers seeking more work.
  • ILO measure: people without a job who have looked for work in the past four weeks and can start within the next two. It comes from the Labour Force Survey, which asks a sample of households about their work.
    • Strength: counts people whether or not they claim, and uses an international definition, so countries can be compared.
    • Weakness: costly, and a sample can be wrong, especially if few households reply.

The two can move differently. Someone whose partner earns too much for them to get benefits can be ILO unemployed without ever appearing as a claimant.

cards.front: Define structural and technological unemployment. A coal mine closes while hospitals in a city 100 miles away are hiring. Why might the miners stay out of work?
cards.back:
Structural unemployment — unemployment caused by the long-term decline of an industry, which leaves workers whose skills or location no longer match the jobs available.

Technological unemployment — unemployment caused by machines or software doing work that people used to do, such as self-service checkouts replacing cashiers. It is a form of structural unemployment: new technology also creates jobs, but usually different ones, needing different skills.

The decline may come from falling demand, new technology or production moving abroad. The miners face two kinds of factor immobility:

  • Occupational immobility: they lack the skills or qualifications for the jobs on offer, and retraining takes time and money.
  • Geographical immobility: they cannot move to where the jobs are, because housing there costs more or they have family ties where they live.

source.verbatim: unemployment caused by the long-term decline of an industry, which leaves workers whose skills or location no longer match the jobs available.

cards.front: Define demand-deficient unemployment and build its chain of reasoning. How would you tell it apart from structural unemployment in a case study, and why does it matter?
cards.back:
Demand-deficient unemployment — unemployment caused by too little aggregate demand. It rises in a recession, so it is also called cyclical unemployment.

The chain: households and firms spend less → firms sell less → they need fewer workers, because labour is a derived demand → they stop hiring and make redundancies → the newly unemployed spend less, and the cycle deepens.

Telling them apart:

  • Job losses across many industries during a recession are demand-deficient.
  • Job losses in one declining industry or region, while other sectors are hiring, are structural.

Why it matters: the cure is different. More spending helps demand-deficient unemployment, but only retraining or new local jobs help structural unemployment.

Frictional unemployment, the short gaps while people move between jobs, is usually brief and is not one of the causes the spec lists.

source.verbatim: unemployment caused by too little aggregate demand. It rises in a recession, so it is also called cyclical unemployment

cards.front: Evaluate the impact of rising unemployment on firms and on individuals.
cards.back:
Firms:

  • Lower sales: people lose their jobs and others fear for theirs → household income and confidence fall → spending falls, especially on luxuries → lower sales and profit. Discount retailers can gain as shoppers trade down.
  • Cheaper recruitment: more applicants for each vacancy → jobs are easier to fill and there is less pressure to raise pay → lower labour costs.

Individuals:

  • Loss of income: a worker loses their job → they rely on savings, benefits or borrowing → their real income and living standards fall.
  • Lost skills: the longer someone is out of work → the more their skills and confidence fade → the harder it is to get hired → lower pay even after they find work. Firms that hire them face higher training costs.
  • Health: money worries and losing a routine → stress and poorer mental health.

It depends on how long it lasts and where it is concentrated. Structural unemployment hits one town or region, so local shops and suppliers suffer most, while firms elsewhere barely notice.

Judgement: a short spell between jobs does little lasting harm. Long-term unemployment does the most damage, because it erodes skills and income, and the harm is greatest where job losses are concentrated in one place.

cards.front: Define macroeconomic objectives. Name the four in the spec, how each is measured and what the UK aims for.
cards.back:
Macroeconomic objectives — the goals a government sets for the performance of the whole economy.

  • Economic growth: measured by the rise in real GDP each year. The aim is steady growth close to the trend rate, because growth far above trend tends to end in rising inflation and then a downturn.
  • Low unemployment: measured by the ILO unemployment rate. The aim is as low as possible, though it can never reach zero, because some people are always moving between jobs.
  • Low and stable inflation: measured by the annual change in the CPI. The aim is 2%, the target the government gives the Bank of England.
  • Current account equilibrium: measured by the current account balance, often as a % of GDP. The aim is a balance that is roughly even over time, with no large deficit or surplus.

The government sets the objectives, and the Bank of England is in charge of inflation. Governments have other aims too, such as a sound budget, a fairer spread of income and protecting the environment, but the spec names these four.

source.verbatim: the goals a government sets for the performance of the whole economy.

cards.front: Define the balance of payments and the current account. What is a current account deficit, and how is it different from a budget deficit?
cards.back:
Balance of payments — the record of all money flowing into and out of a country from its dealings with the rest of the world.

Current account — the part of the balance of payments that records trade in goods and services, plus income such as profits and interest earned abroad and transfers such as foreign aid.

  • Deficit: more money flows out than in, mainly because imports are worth more than exports.
  • Surplus: more money flows in than out.
  • Equilibrium: a balance close to even over several years, not exactly zero in each one.

Not a budget deficit. The current account is about trade and income flows with other countries. A budget deficit is the government spending more than it raises in tax. A country can have one without the other, so check which one the question is asking about.

source.verbatim: the record of all money flowing into and out of a country from its dealings with the rest of the world.

cards.front: Build the chains of reasoning: why do economic growth and low unemployment matter to firms, households and the government?
cards.back:
Economic growth:

  • Firms: real GDP rises → households and other firms spend more → higher sales and profit → more reason to invest in new capacity.
  • Households: more output → more jobs and rising pay → higher real incomes and living standards.
  • The government: higher incomes and profits → more tax revenue at the same tax rates → more to spend on public services, or less borrowing.

Low unemployment:

  • Individuals: a job → a wage instead of benefits → higher income, and skills kept up to date.
  • Firms: more people in work → more customers with money to spend → higher sales. But staff get harder to find, which pushes up wages.
  • The government: fewer people out of work → less spent on benefits and more income tax collected → a smaller budget deficit.

cards.front: Why does the inflation objective say low and stable? Build a chain for each word, and explain why the target is 2% rather than zero.
cards.back:
The government sets the Bank of England a target of 2% CPI inflation, and the Bank sets interest rates to hit it.

  • Low: prices rise slowly → wages and savings keep their value → real incomes hold up, and UK goods stay competitive abroad.
  • Stable: firms can predict their costs and prices → they can plan, sign contracts and agree pay rises with confidence → more investment.

Why not zero? Falling prices bring their own problems: households put off buying in the hope of lower prices later → firms' sales fall.

cards.front: Evaluate whether a large, lasting current account deficit is a problem for the UK.
cards.back:
Why it can be a problem:

  • It has to be paid for: a deficit → the country borrows from abroad or sells assets to foreign buyers → future interest and profits flow overseas.
  • It can cost jobs: households buy imports instead of UK goods → UK producers lose sales → fewer jobs in manufacturing and other traded industries.

It depends on:

  • What the imports are: imported equipment that raises output later, such as robots for a car plant, is easier to justify than imported consumer goods.
  • How it is financed: foreign firms building factories in the UK bring jobs, while short-term borrowing can leave the country quickly.

A large surplus is not the aim either: other countries then run matching deficits, and they may respond with tariffs.

Judgement: a deficit that buys equipment and is financed by foreign firms building in the UK is less worrying than one that pays for consumer goods with short-term borrowing, though interest and profits still flow overseas either way.

cards.front: Define a policy instrument. Name the four instruments in the spec, who runs each one and what it changes.
cards.back:
Policy instrument — a tool the government or the central bank uses to steer the economy towards its objectives.

  • Fiscal policy: run by the government (the Chancellor, in the Budget). Changes government spending and taxes.
  • Monetary policy: run by the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee. Changes Bank Rate, which other interest rates follow.
  • Supply-side policies: run mainly by the government. Change taxes, benefits, training, grants and subsidies, and infrastructure.
  • Exchange rate policy: the government lets the pound float, so nothing is changed: the market sets the rate.

Fiscal and monetary policy change aggregate demand, the total spending in the economy. Supply-side policies raise the economy's capacity to produce.

source.verbatim: a tool the government or the central bank uses to steer the economy towards its objectives

cards.front: Define fiscal policy. Build the chains: how does an expansionary fiscal policy affect firms, and what limits its effect?
cards.back:
Fiscal policy — changing the levels of government spending and taxation to affect aggregate demand.

Expansionary fiscal policy means spending more or taxing less, which raises AD. Contractionary fiscal policy does the opposite, to slow the economy or cut government borrowing. Spending above tax revenue in a year is a budget deficit, covered by borrowing.

  • Government spending rises: on, say, flood defences or a new prison → contracts for builders and their suppliers → more output and more jobs.
  • Income tax or VAT is cut: more take-home pay, or lower prices → households spend more → higher sales for shops and restaurants.
  • Corporation tax is cut: firms keep more profit after tax → more to invest.

It depends on:

  • Whether households spend or save: if confidence is low, a tax cut is saved and sales barely move.
  • How it is paid for: spending funded by borrowing adds to the national debt and its interest, which may mean higher taxes later.
  • Spare capacity: if firms are already near full capacity, extra demand raises prices more than output.

source.verbatim: changing the levels of government spending and taxation to affect aggregate demand.

cards.front: Define monetary policy. Build the chains: how does a rise in Bank Rate affect households, firms and exporters? What decides how hard it bites?
cards.back:
Monetary policy — changing interest rates to affect aggregate demand.

The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee sets Bank Rate to keep CPI inflation at the government's 2% target. Banks' rates on loans, mortgages and savings follow it.

  • Households: mortgage and loan repayments go up and saving pays more → less spending → lower sales, worst for goods often bought on credit, such as new kitchens.
  • Firms: loans and overdrafts cost more → higher costs, and fewer projects worth borrowing for → less investment.
  • Exporters: higher UK rates attract savings from abroad → the pound tends to rise → UK goods cost more overseas → export sales fall.

Together these lower AD, which brings inflation down. A cut in Bank Rate works the other way.

It depends on:

  • How much people and firms borrow: a firm with no debt feels little, and one with cash in the bank gains from higher rates.
  • Fixed or variable rates: many mortgages and business loans are fixed for some years, so the change arrives only when the deal ends.
  • Time lags: the Bank of England says a change usually takes up to two years to have its full effect on inflation.

source.verbatim: changing interest rates to affect aggregate demand.

cards.front: Define supply-side policies. Name the five the spec lists, with the chain for each. How can one tax cut be two kinds of policy?
cards.back:
Supply-side policies — policies that raise the economy's capacity to produce, by improving the quantity or quality of its workers and capital or how well markets work.

  • Taxes: lower income tax → work pays more → more people take jobs or work longer hours → a larger workforce.
  • Benefits: lower benefits or stricter rules for claiming → a bigger gap between income in and out of work → more people look for jobs → firms find it easier to recruit.
  • Education and training: more spending on skills and apprenticeships → workers can do more skilled jobs → higher productivity, lower unit costs and less occupational immobility.
  • Grants and subsidies: money towards research, new equipment or starting a business → lower costs of investing → more innovation and new firms.
  • Infrastructure: better roads, rail and broadband → goods and staff move faster and more cheaply → lower costs and access to wider markets.

One tax cut, two policies: a cut in income tax raises take-home pay, so it is fiscal policy boosting AD in the short run. It also makes work pay more, so it is a supply-side policy raising the workforce over time. Say which effect you mean, and over what time period.

Limits: they take years to work, people may not respond (a firm may take a grant for an investment it would have made anyway), and cutting benefits leaves those who cannot work poorer.

source.verbatim: policies that raise the economy's capacity to produce, by improving the quantity or quality of its workers and capital or how well markets work.

cards.front: Define a floating exchange rate. Evaluate the UK's choice to let the pound float, for the economy and for firms.
cards.back:
Floating exchange rate — an exchange rate set by the demand for and supply of a currency on the foreign exchange market, with no target from the government or central bank.

Under a fixed exchange rate, the central bank would instead buy and sell its currency to hold an agreed value.

How a floating pound helps the economy:

  • It adjusts on its own: the UK buys more imports than it sells exports → more pounds are sold → the pound falls → exports get cheaper abroad and imports dearer → the deficit narrows.
  • It leaves interest rates free: the Bank does not have to set rates to defend the pound → it can set them for the 2% inflation target.

The cost for firms is uncertainty: the pound moves → an exporter's revenue and an importer's costs in pounds change from month to month → margins are harder to predict → some firms hold back on investment, or pay their bank to fix a rate months ahead.

It depends on how much the firm trades abroad. A hairdresser with UK suppliers hardly notices, while a firm that imports components and exports finished machines is exposed on both sides.

Judgement: for the economy, a floating pound tends to narrow a trade deficit on its own and frees interest rates for the inflation target. The cost is uncertainty, and it falls mostly on firms that trade heavily abroad.

source.verbatim: an exchange rate set by the demand for and supply of a currency on the foreign exchange market, with no target from the government or central bank.

cards.front: Sketch the short-run Phillips curve. Explain the trade-off it shows, and when that trade-off breaks down.
cards.back:
Trade-off — a situation where getting more of one thing means accepting less of another.

Short-run Phillips curve — a curve showing an inverse relationship between the rate of inflation and the rate of unemployment in the short run.

Inflation (%) is on the vertical axis and unemployment (%) on the horizontal. The SRPC falls steeply at low unemployment, then flattens out as unemployment rises.

  • Cutting unemployment: AD rises → firms hire more and spare workers become scarce → firms raise wages to recruit and pass the cost on in prices → inflation rises.
  • Cutting inflation: Bank Rate rises → households and firms spend less → firms cut output and stop hiring → unemployment rises.

The trade-off is not fixed. It depends on:

  • The cause of inflation: cost-push inflation, such as a jump in energy prices, can raise inflation and unemployment together, so the curve gives no guide.
  • Spare capacity: in a deep recession, extra demand creates jobs with little effect on prices.
  • The time period: supply-side policies that raise productivity can lower both over the long run.
cards.svgAlt: Inflation (%) on the vertical axis and unemployment (%) on the horizontal; a curve labelled SRPC slopes down, steep where unemployment is low and almost flat where unemployment is high

source.verbatim: a curve showing an inverse relationship between the rate of inflation and the rate of unemployment in the short run.

cards.front: Define a negative externality. Build the chains: why does economic growth tend to raise these costs, and why does the conflict run both ways?
cards.back:
Negative externality — a cost of producing or consuming a good that falls on a third party, who is not paid for it, such as pollution from a factory.

  • Pollution: more output → more energy, transport and raw materials used → more emissions and waste → costs for people living nearby and for the climate.
  • Congestion: more people commuting and more goods moved → busier roads → longer journeys and higher transport costs for firms.
  • The other way round: policies that cut externalities, such as carbon taxes or tighter regulation → firms' costs rise → growth can slow in the short run.

How sharp the conflict is depends on:

  • The kind of growth: growth in services, or in clean energy, adds far less pollution than growth in heavy industry.
  • The time period: green investment costs firms money now but can create new industries and jobs later.

source.verbatim: a cost of producing or consuming a good that falls on a third party, who is not paid for it, such as pollution from a factory.

cards.front: Even with a clear objective, why is managing the economy hard? Give six problems governments face, with the chain for each.
cards.back:
• Conflicting objectives: faster growth → more spending on imports → a wider current account deficit. Cutting the budget deficit → less spending → slower growth. The government has to choose which objective matters most at the time.
  • Time lags: a change in Bank Rate can take up to two years to work in full → by then, the economy may have moved on.
  • Late and uncertain data: GDP figures arrive weeks after the quarter ends and are often revised → policy-makers can misjudge where the economy is.
  • Shocks from abroad: a world recession or a rise in oil prices → hits the UK whatever its own policies.
  • Limited money: extra spending or tax cuts have to be paid for → a large national debt limits how much more the government can borrow.
  • Politics: tax rises and spending cuts are unpopular → they may be delayed, especially before an election.

cards.front: The UK enters a recession and unemployment is rising. What would a Keynesian economist and a free-market economist each advise, and why do they disagree?
cards.back:
They disagree about how the economy works, so they recommend different policies.

  • Keynesian: the economy can stay below full capacity for years if spending is weak, so the main worry is unemployment and lost output. Advice: the government borrows to spend, on projects such as new schools and flood defences, to replace the missing demand, and spends on training and infrastructure.
  • Free-market: left alone, markets return the economy to full capacity fairly quickly, so the main worries are inflation, high taxes and government debt. Advice: avoid adding to debt, use monetary policy for inflation, and cut taxes and red tape so that firms expand.

Role of government: Keynesians want a large one, managing demand to keep output near capacity. Free-market economists want a small one: keep inflation low and let markets work.

cards.front: Define an unintended consequence. UK inflation is rising because world gas prices have jumped. Evaluate raising Bank Rate in response.
cards.back:
Unintended consequence — an effect of a policy that policy-makers did not aim for, often on another objective or another group.

Match the instrument to the cause, not just the problem. Here the cause is world energy prices, and a higher Bank Rate works by cutting demand:

  • How it would work: Bank Rate rises → households and firms borrow and spend less → prices rise more slowly, but only by cutting spending and jobs.
  • Unintended consequences: slower growth and job losses, and a stronger pound that hurts exporters.

It also depends on:

  • How people respond: households and firms may change their behaviour in ways no one planned.
  • Using instruments together: if the government loosens fiscal policy while the Bank is raising rates, the two pull against each other.

Other matches: a recession → more government spending or tax cuts (risk: more debt and more imports). A skills shortage → education and training (risk: firms cut their own training and let the state pay). Low investment → a cut in corporation tax (risk: higher dividends instead, and less tax revenue).

Judgement: higher interest rates do little against inflation caused by world energy prices, and slow it mainly by costing growth and jobs. Name the cause, pick the instrument that tackles it, then name one unintended consequence.

source.verbatim: an effect of a policy that policy-makers did not aim for, often on another objective or another group.
